source.title: Signatures of Steerability in Activation Space of Language Models

page_placements.theme: Geometric measures, task values and causal interpretation

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a synthetic superposition experiment, but constructs the feature dictionary rather than testing whether a network learns the claimed storage geometry. Its results concern how separation metrics correlate with properties of that constructed setup, not whether the claim's representational geometry occurs.
record.gate_note: The synthetic experiment reports correlations between separation metrics and dictionary coherence, active noise-feature count, and alignment with a designated feature. The dictionary geometry is specified by construction; the paper does not train a network to test feature storage or its geometric transitions. Real-model results concern steering correlations, not the claim versions about feature representation.
record.test_reason: The study uses a hand-built superposition dictionary, with set coherence ϵ and active-feature count k, to interpret its own separation metrics for steering. No network is trained, so nothing shows whether features come to be stored in superposition. Its real-LLM results correlate CAA steerability with activation-separation statistics; they measure no feature spread, SAE recovery, polysemanticity or feature dimensionality. The record's discusses/T6 undersells this: superposition is used as a tool to validate the study's own metrics, which is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct but incomplete. It should add the main result: across six LLMs and 38 datasets, simple separation statistics, especially SNR, strongly predict CAA steerability even after controlling for layer and dataset. The synthetic result is that the metrics track feature recovery strongly and global superposition structure only weakly. The authors state the analyses are correlational, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: The paper builds a synthetic dictionary with specified coherence and sparsified noise coefficients to study metric correlations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-learning experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The synthetic structural parameters vary across ambient dimension, dictionary-size ratio, target coherence, active-feature count, and class mean-gap; the within-configuration analysis uses 20 data points per configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: In a constructed sparse dictionary, SNR and mean alignment track recovery of the target direction π (ρ≈0.91) but barely track k (ρ≈-0.33) and not ϵ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In synthetic superposition, contrastive separation metrics index target-direction recovery more than global sparsity or coherence.

fits_no_version.finding: Within fixed configurations, the SNR and mean-alignment association with π persists (median 0.92), while intrinsic dimension's association vanishes (median 0.006).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intrinsic dimension tracks between-regime geometry rather than feature recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: In six instruction-tuned LLMs, SNR correlates with CAA steerability (r≈0.69–0.82) and still does so after controlling for layer and dataset; these results are not in the rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation separation of contrastive sets predicts linear steerability.

record.problems: The superposition results come from a constructed synthetic dictionary rather than trained networks. The paper says its main analyses are correlational, not causal. It limits its real-model steering evaluation to multiple-choice option logits and does not test free-form fluency or unrelated-task performance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported synthetic-superposition correlations were left out; repeated pooled estimates in Table 13 and repeated values in confidence-interval tables were not duplicated.

untested.parts: All: no network is trained. Overlapping near-orthogonal storage, a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry are set by construction or not examined.
All: no neurons or capacity allocation are studied.
All: LLM activations are used only for CAA steering-vector statistics; there is no SAE and no measure of features spread across neurons.
All: no SAE or dictionary learning is applied to models.
All: the study assumes concepts are 1-D directions (LRH) and does not test this against multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) is invoked as background and built into a synthetic generator to explain the study's metrics, not tested. The real-model steering tables (Tables 1–11) bear on no superposition version and need no rows.

versions.untested_parts: Whether networks store more sparse features than dimensions as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; whether there is a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry; and whether feature importance changes that geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or gives important features dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure, and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons or can be recovered with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representations.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relation.reason: Superposition supplies the synthetic setup for assessing separation metrics against known feature recovery; the real-model experiments measure correlations with CAA steerability.

tranche.reason: Sections 3.4 and 4.2 use a constructed superposition dictionary to evaluate steering diagnostics. They do not test whether networks learn superposition or establish any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Table 13 and Appendix F support all four rows and the cited statement. The dictionary structure is imposed; these metric correlations do not measure learned superposition, and the authors explicitly describe their analyses as correlative.
